title: The Relationship Advice Jesus Would Give Today
paragraphs:
The Relationship Advice Jesus Would Give Today
The Words Modern Relationships Desperately Need to Hear Before It's Too Late
What if the greatest relationship counselor who ever lived sat across from you today?
Not in a church pew.
Not on a stage.
Not through a viral quote posted on social media.
But face-to-face.
Looking directly into the wounds you've hidden from everyone else.
The heartbreak.
The betrayal.
The loneliness inside a marriage nobody suspects is struggling.
The situationship that keeps breaking your spirit.
The anxiety of being single.
The disappointment of loving someone who refuses to love you back.
The exhaustion of giving everything and receiving almost nothing.
What would Jesus say?
Would He give dating tips?
Would He teach communication strategies?
Would He explain love languages?
Perhaps.
But before Jesus addressed your relationship with another person, He would first address the relationship that governs every other relationship in your life.
Your relationship with Him.
That is the part modern culture keeps trying to skip.
And it is why so many people are starving emotionally while drowning in advice.
Because no relationship can consistently give what only God was designed to provide.
The greatest relationship crisis today is not merely between husbands and wives.
It is not between boyfriends and girlfriends.
It is not between parents and children.
It is between humanity and God.
Until that relationship is healed, every other relationship carries a weight it was never created to bear.
When Jesus was asked about the greatest commandment, He answered:
"You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind."
(Matthew 22:37)
In the Greek text, the word used for love is ἀγαπήσεις (agapēseis)—a self-giving, sacrificial, covenantal love.
Then Jesus immediately added:
"You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
(Matthew 22:39)
Notice the order.
Love God first.
Love people second.
Modern relationships often reverse the order.
People search for identity in romance.
Purpose in romance.
Healing in romance.
Security in romance.
Salvation in romance.
But another human being was never meant to be your savior.
Only Jesus can carry that burden.
That is why some of the most painful words people say are:
"I thought they would complete me."
No human being can complete what only God can restore.
The first relationship advice Jesus would give today would likely sound shocking:
Stop asking another person to be your god.
Many relationships collapse because expectations become idolatry.
The partner becomes the source of happiness.
The source of validation.
The source of peace.
The source of identity.
The source of worth.
When they fail—as every imperfect human eventually will—the entire foundation collapses.
Jesus would lovingly expose that foundation before it destroys you.
Because He loves you too much to let you build your life on something that cannot hold your weight.
The ancient Hebrew Scriptures contain a powerful word:
חֶסֶד (chesed)
It is often translated as lovingkindness, steadfast love, covenant love, mercy, or faithful devotion.
No single English word fully captures its depth.
It describes the unwavering faithfulness of God toward undeserving people.
The kind of love that remains when feelings fluctuate.
The kind of love that continues when circumstances change.
The kind of love that pursues when others abandon.
Most people are searching for chesed in human relationships without first receiving it from God.
But once you encounter God's covenant love, something changes.
You stop demanding perfection from people.
Because you finally understand that you were never perfect either.
One of the most overlooked relationship teachings of Jesus appears in Luke 6:31:
"And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them."
Simple.
Yet revolutionary.
Imagine if every argument began there.
Imagine if every text message began there.
Imagine if every marriage practiced that daily.
Imagine if every breakup honored that principle.
Imagine if every disagreement submitted to those words.
The world would look radically different.
Because Jesus consistently shifted attention away from what others owed us and toward how we should love others.
Not because abuse should be tolerated.
Not because boundaries do not matter.
Not because wisdom should be ignored.
But because transformation begins with personal surrender, not personal entitlement.
And perhaps nowhere is Jesus' relationship advice more countercultural than His teaching on forgiveness.
Some readers are already uncomfortable.
Because someone hurt you.
Deeply.
Maybe they betrayed your trust.
Maybe they walked away.
Maybe they cheated.
Maybe they lied.
Maybe they abandoned their promises.
Maybe the wounds still ache years later.
And yet Jesus said:
"Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors."
(Matthew 6:12)
The Greek word translated forgive is ἀφίημι (aphiēmi).
It literally carries the idea of releasing, letting go, sending away.
Forgiveness is not pretending evil never happened.
It is refusing to remain chained to what happened.
Forgiveness does not always restore a relationship.
But it restores freedom to the wounded heart.
Jesus knows that bitterness feels powerful.
But He also knows it slowly becomes a prison.
And prisons rarely look like prisons while we are building them.
Many people reading this are carrying names in their hearts they have never released.
The person may not even remember what they did.
Yet they still occupy emotional space rent-free.
Jesus would gently ask:
How much longer do you want to carry them?
Not because their actions were acceptable.
But because your freedom matters.
The world says, "Protect your heart."
Jesus says:
"Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."
(Matthew 5:8)
The world says, "Get even."
Jesus says:
"Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you."
(Matthew 5:44)
The world says, "Follow your heart."
Jesus says:
"Follow Me."
Those are radically different destinations.
Because hearts can be deceived.
Feelings can fluctuate.
Desires can mislead.
But Christ never changes.
The deepest relationship advice Jesus would give today is not about finding the right person.
It is about becoming the right person through surrender to Him.
Because healthy relationships are often the fruit of transformed hearts.
Not merely compatible personalities.
Not merely chemistry.
Not merely attraction.
Transformation.
There is another word Jesus used repeatedly:
μετάνοια (metanoia)
Usually translated as repentance.
Yet repentance is far more than feeling guilty.
Metanoia means a change of mind that produces a change of direction.
A turning.
A reorientation.
A new path.
In relationships, many people want different results without different directions.
Jesus offers both.
He transforms the heart that keeps choosing destruction.
The heart that keeps running from commitment.
The heart that keeps sabotaging intimacy.
The heart that keeps seeking validation from broken places.
And that is why the Gospel remains the greatest relationship story ever told.
Because it begins with scandal.
Humanity rebelled.
Humanity wandered.
Humanity sinned.
Humanity chose darkness.
Yet grace came searching anyway.
The cross is the ultimate relationship restoration story.
God pursuing people who did not deserve pursuit.
God loving people who did not earn love.
God forgiving people who could never repay the debt.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
That is scandal.
That is grace.
That is Jesus rewriting everything.
Perhaps that is what you need to hear today.
Not that your relationship situation is hopeless.
Not that your past disqualifies you.
Not that your failures define you.
Not that your wounds are the end of your story.
Because Jesus specializes in rewriting stories everyone else has given up on.
He rewrote Peter's story after denial.
He rewrote Paul's story after persecution.
He rewrote the Samaritan woman's story after shame.
He rewrote the thief's story while hanging on a cross.
And He can rewrite yours too.
Maybe your greatest relationship breakthrough will not begin with finding someone.
Maybe it will begin with finding Christ more deeply than ever before.
Because when Jesus becomes your first love, every other love finds its proper place.
If this article spoke to your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Your testimony may encourage someone else more than you realize.
One practical way believers can participate in that mission is by supporting and sharing faithful Gospel-centered work so more people can encounter God's Word.
Because one shared article can reach a searching soul.
One comment can encourage a weary believer.
One testimony can point someone toward Christ.
And one act of faithfulness can echo into eternity.
The relationship you have been searching for may not begin when someone finally chooses you.
It may begin the moment you fully realize that Jesus already did.
